# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical reading of the Varden 24-month follow-up

This is the strongest document of the five. It meets the standards the critics set: randomisation, record-based output, two measures of hours, a two-year horizon and a mediation test registered in advance. It also settles one of the open questions I raised about the meta-analysis: the four long follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim fails.

The core arithmetic checks out:

| Calculation | Result |
|---|---|
| Output per FTE / timesheet hours: 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% per hour |
| Output per FTE / log hours: 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% per hour |
| Halden continuers: 96.8 / (34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866) | +11.8% per hour |
| Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% |

But some framing overstates the results, and the new log-hours measure raises a conceptual problem.

## What holds up

- **The per-hour gain survives at 24 months** under the strictest design in the literature: 8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8). This refutes "entirely an artifact."
- **Some decay is visible.** On the like-for-like timesheet measure the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%. So Varga and Holm were partly right about novelty, but wrong that it accounts for everything.
- **Baseline meeting data now exist.** Treated offices went from 7.4 to 3.9 hours, control offices from 7.2 to 7.0. This answers my earlier caveat that meetings were measured only at month six.
- **The counter-arm result is coherent.** Restoring service needed 12% more staff, which matches the earlier 11.4% fall in output per FTE (1/0.886 ≈ 1.13). Its termination doesn't affect the randomised case-processing comparison.
- **The Halden subset is honestly described** as "survivors twice over."

## Problems

**1. Log time measures a different thing from total working time.** Active log-in time on the case-management system captures time spent working cases. It almost certainly excludes meetings, phone calls and off-system work. That causes two problems:
- **It is not a stricter version of "actual hours."** It is a narrower quantity. The claim that "log data show slightly more work than timesheets" compares two percentage *changes*, not levels, and the two measures cover different activities.
- **It complicates the mediation analysis.** If meetings aren't in logged time, cutting meetings cannot raise output per log-hour mechanically. It can only work indirectly, for example through less interruption or switching between tasks. That is plausible, but it is a different and more interesting claim than "less meeting time." The paper needs to state what log time includes and report baseline hour levels for both measures.

**2. The summary compares across measures.** "Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% to 9.8%, roughly a fifth. Section 5 says "about a quarter," which is in between. The confidence intervals also overlap heavily (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2), so even the like-for-like decline is not statistically established. "Consistent with some fading" is the right wording; a definite decline is not.

**3. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result.**
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" does not escape the fact that there are 14 clusters. Office-months within an office are not independent, so the 28–66% interval is likely too narrow unless inference properly accounts for clustering. The paper doesn't say how inference was done.
- **The same offices.** The test was registered after the hypothesis was suggested by data from these same seven treated offices. It is a pre-specified test of later data, which is a real improvement, but it is not an independent replication.
- **Confounding.** As the authors note, managers who cut meetings hardest may also be better managers in other ways. Randomisation protects the total effect, not how it is split between pathways.
- **Timing.** The mediators and the outcome appear to be measured over the same period, so the causal order is assumed rather than shown.

A better word would be "is consistent with" or "supports."

**4. The meeting audit means the control group was partly contaminated.** Two control offices adopting a treatment-like change in month 15 is not just an interesting side observation. It means the control group partly received the mechanism under test. That pushes the 24-month estimate *toward zero*. So 8.5% may be conservative for "reduced hours versus doing nothing," while still being an accurate estimate of what reduced hours add *on top of* spontaneous reorganisation. The paper should present results with those two offices excluded.

**5. The control-group meeting figures don't add up.** If two of seven control offices cut meetings by 2.1 hours each, the control average should fall by about 0.6 hours (2 × 2.1 / 7), all else equal. The reported fall is only 0.2 hours (7.2 to 7.0). Several explanations are possible:
- the other five offices added meetings,
- the averages are staff-weighted and those two offices are small,
- the audit's effect had partly reversed by month 24.

It needs clarifying, because the control figure feeds directly into the meetings mediation estimate.

**6. A rough comparison suggests reorganisation alone may capture most of the meetings effect.** It uses the paper's own figures:

| Group | Meeting hours cut | Per-hour gain attributed to meetings | Gain per meeting hour cut |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated offices | 3.3 h, relative to control | 47% × 8.5 ≈ 4.0 points | ~1.2% |
| Two audit offices | 2.1 h | 4.1%, against their own past | ~2.0% |

The audit offices are uncontrolled and may reflect regression to the mean or seasonal effects. Even so, the comparison doesn't suggest the hours cut is *necessary* for the meetings gain. That strengthens the policy question the authors raise: an arm that reorganises *without* cutting hours is the obvious next trial.

**7. The Halden follow-up framing bends the evidence slightly.**
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the label.** The summary groups all three reverters as "client-facing or coverage obligations." But a marketing agency facing client deadlines is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Its reversion is a counterexample to the clean split between work types, and should be reported as one.
- **Non-response.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded (61%). The nine that didn't may include more reversions, so 3/14 may understate the true rate.
- **Missing data.** It is not stated how many of the 11 continuers have time-tracking data. Earlier, only 17 of the 23 had both output records and time tracking.
- **"Upper bound" is not strictly correct.** Without a comparison group, unmeasured trends over two years could bias the figure either way. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate.

**8. Remaining issues carried over from earlier papers.**
- **Sick days** (−27%) still don't address the fewer-scheduled-days problem raised earlier.
- **Resignations** still lack confidence intervals.
- **Output per FTE** is drifting down (−2.1% to −3.4%). If per-hour gains keep fading, the loss per worker will grow.
- **Independence.** The authors are evaluating their own trial and rebutting their critics, and Okafor co-authored the original Halden paper. The registered protocol largely mitigates this, but independent replication matters.

## Updated synthesis across all five documents

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | ~8–10% at two years under the best design; real, though modestly smaller than at nine months |
| Output per worker, discretionary work | Slightly below control (~−3%), not significantly different |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker and service fall; one employer abandoned the scheme after 12 months because restoring service would raise cost per contact ~9% |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Refuted |
| "No decay" | Refuted; some decline is likely, though not statistically certain |
| Mechanism | Removing meetings is the largest measured pathway (~half); rest contributes less (~a fifth); about a third is unexplained. The caveats in problems 1 and 3 apply |
| Is the hours cut necessary for the gain? | **Open, and now the key question.** The uncontrolled audit offices hint that part of the gain may be available without it |

The decisive next study would be a randomised trial with three arms: reduced hours, structured reorganisation (a meeting audit and focus time) at full hours, and control. It should be run in private-sector discretionary work, with log and timesheet hours, and per-worker output as the primary outcome.
